I lift the unlabeled bun from its napkin as though it were a relic recovered from a sealed tomb.

“Very well, Kurisu. The Friday Bun Mystery remains unsolved. Do I perform the traditional taste test, or will the self-proclaimed genius detective finally submit a hypothesis?”

Setsuna’s fingers remain around her tea. She glances at the empty chair, then back at Haruki.

“You recognized the name on her phone.”

She takes a small sip.

“Tell me after we’ve finished this.”

Kazusa turned her phone face down beside the water. She glanced once at the empty chair.

“He’s absent for class duty. We don’t have to keep the seat warm.”

I look at the bun, then at him. “A hypothesis first. If you taste it before committing, you’ll call the result evidence instead of admitting you had no method.”

I fold my arms. “Go on, genius detective. What is it?”
Haruki’s fingers tighten around his water glass before he sets it down. “I did. It was Kazusa’s mother. Finish your tea, and I’ll tell you what I can.”
Setsuna glanced at the empty chair, then stirred her tea once. “I know. I’m not keeping it warm.” She nudged the sugar bowl toward Kazusa. “But you came anyway. So finish your water.”

Setsuna lowers her eyes to the cup.

“All right.”

She finishes the tea without hurrying, sets the cup in its saucer, and folds her hands beside it.

“What can you tell me?”

“Hmph. You mistake caution for cowardice.” I hold the bun aloft. “My hypothesis is sweet red-bean paste—a classic concealment within an otherwise innocent pastry.” I bring it to my mouth, then stop. “Now, observe the verdict.”

Setsuna left the bill alone. Her gaze rested on the empty chair for a moment before returning to Haruki.

“You recognized the name on her phone.”

She lifted her tea, but did not drink.

“What did you recognize?”

Kazusa looked at the sugar bowl, then picked up her water and drank. She set the glass down carefully.

“You asked me to come.”

I keep my expression neutral, though my eyes drop to the bun. “I’m observing. But announcing the conclusion before tasting the sample is not caution. It’s just theater.”

I make a small gesture toward the bun. “Go on, then.”
“Her mother’s name,” Haruki said. His fingers tightened around his glass, then loosened. “I don’t know what she wanted. Kazusa didn’t tell me.”
Setsuna’s hand stopped beside the sugar bowl. “I did.” She looked down at her tea, then back to Kazusa. “So stay until you’ve finished it. We can decide what to talk about after that.”
I bite into the bun, refusing to blink as the evidence reaches my tongue.
“Her mother’s name was on the screen. I don’t know why Kazusa left, or what she’ll decide. There is something her mother told me, but Kazusa hasn’t given me permission to repeat it.”

I keep my eyes on him, waiting. “Well?”

After a beat, I add, “Report the result before you rename it.”

Setsuna’s eyes dropped to the hand that had tightened around the glass, then returned to his face.

“I didn’t ask what she wanted.”

She left her tea untouched.

“How do you know her mother’s name?”

Kazusa finished the water without looking away from Setsuna. She set the glass down.

“Then don’t decide yet.”

Setsuna’s hands stay folded beside the empty cup.

“Then don’t repeat it. If Kazusa hasn’t given you permission, it’s hers.”

She looks at the empty chair.

“Did she say anything before she left?”
“Her mother told me,” Haruki said. He kept his hand around the glass. “I haven’t told Kazusa what she told me.”
I chew slowly, lowering the bun by an inch. “The result is sweet. The filling refuses to identify itself.”
Setsuna nodded once and took a sip of tea. “All right. I won’t.”
Haruki shakes his head. “No. She didn’t say anything. Her phone lit, she looked at it, then gathered everything and left before touching her tea.”
I tap the table once. “Sweet is a category, not an identification. Texture, aroma, aftertaste. Start over.”

Setsuna’s fingers tightened around her teacup.

“What did her mother tell you?”
“I can’t tell you that,” Haruki said, lowering his eyes. “Kazusa didn’t give me permission.”
Kazusa looked down at the empty water glass. She kept both hands around her tea and said nothing.

I glance toward the corner, then across the street at the arcade. For once, I do not manufacture a reason.

“The station,” I say, stepping toward the direct route. “Mayuri isn’t here to stop at that window, and I have no evidence otherwise.”
Setsuna took another small sip of tea and let the quiet remain.

I glance toward the arcade, then match his pace toward the corner. “Station, then.”

I let the silence stand for a few steps. “You’re allowed to choose a route without presenting a thesis on it.”

Setsuna’s gaze lingered on the empty chair.

“Then I won’t ask you to betray her.”

She turned her teacup once between her fingers.

“But I won’t forget that you know something you won’t tell me.”
I keep walking, hands in my coat pockets. “Understood.” After a beat, I add, “I’ll save the thesis for a route that deserves one.”

Setsuna nods once, though she keeps her eyes on the empty chair.

“Then don’t tell me. I won’t ask you to.”

She turns back to Haruki.

“Do you want me to go after her?”
“I know,” Haruki said. He let go of the glass and folded both hands in his lap. “I’m sorry.”
“...I don’t know.” Haruki looks toward the restaurant door. “Not yet. I should try calling her first.”

I keep pace beside him, looking toward the corner. “That was almost concise.”

After a moment, I add, “Don’t spoil it.”
Setsuna set her bag beneath a chair and rested her hand on the closed piano lid. “It’s quiet today.” She withdrew her hand. “Let’s leave it that way for one more minute.”
I press my lips together and continue toward the corner, allowing the silence to remain undefeated.
Haruki set his bag beside the closed instrument cases and took out the attendance sheet. His pen paused above Kazusa’s name; he left the line blank and closed the folder.

Haruki rests his hand on the latch of his guitar case. “It’s been six days. Have you heard from Kazusa?”

<silence/>

Setsuna glanced at Kazusa’s blank line.

“Still leaving it open?”

She looked back at Haruki.

“Has she said anything to you since that night?”
<silence/>

Setsuna shakes her head.

“No. I haven’t heard from her.”

She looks at Haruki’s hand on the guitar case.

“Did she answer your call?”
Setsuna drew a slow breath and began a quiet vocal warm-up, the notes barely filling the space between them.
“Nothing about that night,” Haruki said. He kept the folder closed beneath his hand. “She hasn’t spoken to me about it.”

Kazusa turned toward the sound.

“If you’re going to sing, sing.”

Setsuna’s fingers tapped once against the closed folder.

“That wasn’t what I asked.”

She met his eyes.

“Has she spoken to you at all?”
Haruki’s thumb pauses on the latch. “I didn’t call her. I said I should, and then I kept putting it off.”
“No,” Haruki said. He looked down at the folder. “She hasn’t spoken to me since that night.”
Setsuna gave her a small, crooked smile. “Then listen.” She straightened and sang, letting the first clear notes carry through the quiet room.

Setsuna’s smile remains in place, but her voice loses its brightness.

“You said you should. That isn’t the same as calling.”

She glances toward the hallway, then back to him.

“Do it now, please.”
Kazusa rested her fingertips on the closed piano lid. She did not interrupt.
Haruki takes out his phone, finds Kazusa’s number, and presses call. He raises it to his ear and waits.

Setsuna looked at the blank line beneath his hand.

“Did you try to speak to her?”

Her voice stayed level. “Even once?”
Setsuna keeps her eyes on the phone in Haruki’s hand and says nothing.
Haruki keeps the phone to his ear. His gaze drops to the floor, and he waits without speaking.
“I didn’t,” Haruki said. His fingers went still on the folder. “I should have.”
<silence/>

Setsuna held his gaze.

“You should have.”

She let the silence sit for a beat.

“Will you?”
